source.title_on_document: My Way or the AI Way? How Autonomy Frustration Undermines Creative Performance Through Editing AI Advice

supplement.where: Online Supporting Information section of the journal article (p. 14, 'Supporting Information'); data and manipulation check on OSF https://osf.io/qyvj8/overview (p. 5)
supplement.holds: Figure S1: box plot of DAT scores across human, human-ChatGPT-4, and ChatGPT-4 groups with Tukey's HSD group differences (the only place the human-ChatGPT vs human-alone pairwise comparison is reported). Table S1: mediation analysis without covariates.

paper_design_summary: A qualitative prestudy interviewed 26 graduate students about autonomy when using AI. In the main study, 377 German university students completed the Divergent Association Task (DAT); each person chose whether to receive a ChatGPT-4-generated 10-word solution to edit (N = 222) or to work alone (N = 155), so AI use was self-selected, not randomized. The DAT score (computed semantic distance) was compared across the human-alone group, the human-ChatGPT group, and ChatGPT-4 alone, and, within the AI group, related to autonomy frustration and the number of AI words edited; a separate manipulation-check sample (88 of 120 who chose AI) reported decision-making autonomy with and without AI.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing; qualitative interviews about attitudes toward AI, autonomy, and authenticity.
assignment.quote: we conducted a preliminary interview study (Gibson 2016).

arms.name: Interviewees
arms.description: Graduate working students interviewed for 10 to 15 min

participants.who: Graduate students at a large German business school working at least 20 h per week as working students; all had used LLMs such as ChatGPT
participants.quote: Our sample included 26 participants (17 females and nine males) who were 24.4 years old on average (SD = 1.8).

ai_tool.name_model: Not applicable (participants discussed their own use of LLMs such as ChatGPT)
ai_tool.how_used: No AI was used in the study; interviews only.

task.description: Semistructured interview on attitudes toward AI and sense of autonomy and authenticity when using AI.

studies.label: Main study (DAT with optional ChatGPT-4 advice)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned: participants chose whether to receive a ChatGPT-4-generated 10-word DAT solution that they could edit, or to generate their own 10 words.
assignment.quote: participants were given the option to receive AI-generated advice from ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI 2023). Participants who chose to receive the AI advice (N = 222) were presented with a set of 10 AI-generated words

arms.name: Human-ChatGPT (chose AI advice)
arms.description: Shown 10 ChatGPT-4-generated DAT words (horizon, planet, notebook, honesty, chimpanzee, cake, plateau, opera, airplane, gloves) and allowed to edit any number before finalizing

arms.name: Human alone (opted out of AI advice)
arms.description: Generated their own list of 10 words

arms.name: ChatGPT-4 alone
arms.description: Benchmark: 100 unique DAT solutions generated by ChatGPT-4 (M = 85.62, SD = 3.42); not a group of people

participants.exclusions: 397 recruited; 20 excluded due to missing data; no multivariate outliers (Mahalanobis distance). Final sample 377 (222 chose AI advice, 155 opted out). Autonomy frustration and mediation analyses use only the 222 who chose AI advice (Table 1 note N = 222).
participants.who: Students from three large German universities, mostly in part-time (dual) degree courses while employed; recruited through an online portal for course credit; 77.5% female; mean age 24.84; average 26.19 work hours per week
participants.quote: We excluded 20 participants due to missing data, resulting in a final sample of 377 participants

ai_tool.how_used: Participants who opted in received one fixed AI-generated 10-word DAT solution, chosen from 100 ChatGPT-4 solutions as the one closest to the mean score (85.64), and could edit any of the words (footnote 3, p. 10).

task.description: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): produce 10 English nouns as different as possible; score is the transformed average pairwise semantic distance of the first seven valid words.

outcomes.name: DAT score by group (human alone, human-ChatGPT, ChatGPT-4 alone)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT score: algorithmic semantic distance across pairs of the first seven valid words, transformed average (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1.2.2). Compared by one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD post hoc tests.

contrasts.control_arm: Human alone (opted out of AI advice)
contrasts.reported: No direct pairwise statistic in this PDF; the pairwise Tukey HSD result sits in Supporting Information Figure S1. Direction read from the two printed differences against the same ChatGPT-4-alone reference: human alone dM = -7.94, 95% CI [-9.36, -6.52]; human-ChatGPT dM = -4.08, 95% CI [-5.51, -2.65]. Self-selected groups, not randomized. Human-ChatGPT group DAT mean 82.87 (SD 4.51, N = 222, Table 1); no human-alone mean printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, footnote 5; p. 7, Table 1; p. 14, Supporting Information (Figure S1)

contrasts.reported: One-way ANOVA F(2, 402) = 87.24, p < 0.001; human-ChatGPT collaboration group vs ChatGPT-4 alone dM = -4.08, 95% CI [-5.51, -2.65], p < 0.001

contrasts.control_arm: Human alone (opted out of AI advice)
contrasts.reported: Human-alone group vs ChatGPT-4 alone dM = -7.94, 95% CI [-9.36, -6.52], p < 0.001; ChatGPT-4 100 solutions M = 85.62, SD = 3.42

outcomes.name: DAT score related to autonomy frustration and extent of editing among AI-advice participants (mediation)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same DAT score; PROCESS Model 4 mediation (OLS paths, 5000 bootstrap resamples) with gender, age, education, weekly working hours, and prior ChatGPT use as covariates; results without covariates in Table S1 (supplement). Extent of editing = number of the 10 AI words edited (0-10). Autonomy frustration = 3-item METUX TENS-task subscale, 7-point scale.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Higher extent of editing (continuous, within AI-advice group)
contrasts.control_arm: Lower extent of editing (continuous, within AI-advice group)
contrasts.reported: Path b (extent of editing -> DAT): B = -0.621, SE 0.053, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-0.727, -0.515]; correlation r = -0.62 (Table 1). Path a (autonomy frustration -> editing): B = 0.650, SE 0.262, p = 0.014, 95% CI [0.134, 1.17]. Direct effect c' (autonomy frustration -> DAT): B = 0.100, SE 0.208, p = 0.630, 95% CI [-0.310, 0.511]. Indirect effect a x b: B = -0.403, 95% CI [-0.721, -0.084], R2 = 0.404. N = 222.

studies.label: Manipulation check (separate sample; DAT with and without AI advice, self-reported autonomy)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not stated. The 88 participants who chose to receive AI advice completed the DAT with and without AI-generated advice; order of conditions not stated.
assignment.quote: We examined whether the 88 participants ... who chose to receive AI advice in the DAT differed in their reported decision-making autonomy when they completed the DAT with versus without receiving AI-generated advice.

participants.exclusions: 131 students recruited; 11 failed at least one of two attention checks; final sample 120; of these, the 88 who chose AI advice enter the paired comparison.
participants.who: Students from a large German business school (76.7% female, mean age 24.5)
participants.quote: We recruited 131 students from a large German business school. Of these, 11 failed at least one of two attention check items

ai_tool.how_used: AI-generated DAT advice, as in the main study.

task.description: Divergent Association Task completed with and without AI advice; only self-reported decision-making autonomy is reported.

company_involvement.description: Authors at the School of Management, Technical University of Munich; funding: 'The authors have nothing to report.' ChatGPT-4 used as a tool only.

eligibility.reason: Participants self-selected into receiving ChatGPT-4 advice (222 chose it, 155 opted out; pp. 5-6), so AI use was not randomly assigned. The sample (377 analyzed) and the DAT outcome scored on output would otherwise qualify. The manipulation check does not state randomized order and reports only self-reported autonomy. The comparison with ChatGPT-4 alone is ai_vs_human context.

one_line_finding: Among 377 students who self-selected into AI advice or not, both the human-alone group (dM = -7.94, 95% CI [-9.36, -6.52]) and the human-ChatGPT group (dM = -4.08, 95% CI [-5.51, -2.65]) scored lower on the DAT than ChatGPT-4 alone, and among AI users more editing of the AI words predicted lower DAT scores (B = -0.621, p < 0.001) (p. 10 footnote 5; p. 7 Table 2).
open_questions: The ANOVA reports F(2, 402), implying 405 observations, which matches neither the 377 people (plus 100 ChatGPT-4 solutions = 477) nor 377 alone; how many ChatGPT-4-alone observations entered the ANOVA is not stated.
The direct human-ChatGPT vs human-alone pairwise test and the human-alone DAT mean appear only in Supporting Information Figure S1, which is not in this PDF.
Whether the order of with-AI and without-AI conditions in the manipulation check was randomized is not stated.
notes: Three studies: a qualitative prestudy (26 interviewees), the main quasi-experimental study (377 analyzed), and a manipulation check on a separate sample (120 analyzed, 88 in the paired comparison). Not listed as outcomes: extent of editing (number of AI words changed, a behavioral mediator, not a creativity score) and self-reported autonomy frustration and decision-making autonomy (self-report). Ethics statement mentions 'the three studies'.
